statement: A UI surface that lets an operator act as, or on behalf of, more than one principal/agent within the SAME mounted component instance MUST key every mutable per-request field (input/intent, in-flight/loading flag, result/outcome, and any error) on the exact composite (principalId, requestSubjectId) pair, never on the request subject alone. A completion handler for an async request MUST write only to the (principalId, requestSubjectId) key captured at the moment the request began — never re-derived from 'whichever principal is selected now' — so a response resolving after the operator switches principals cannot be attributed to the newly selected one. Switching the selected principal MUST NOT clear or reset any other principal's own composite-keyed state; isolation is achieved by keying, never by clearing.
classification: A state-shape defect: per-request UI state was modeled as if there were exactly one implicit consumer, when the surface actually serves multiple concurrently-selectable principals. The generic shape is any component keyed on 'the thing being acted upon' when it should be keyed on '(who is acting, the thing being acted upon)'.

canaries.assertion: Nakamoto's Advisor intent/outcome is invisible under a Kn0w1 selection and vice versa; a request whose completion action carries the agentId captured at REQUEST_START writes only under that agentId even if SELECT_AGENT fires an intervening switch before the completion action is dispatched; switching back to Nakamoto restores exactly the state that was present before the switch.

occurrences.defect: intents/outcomes/requesting/serviceErrors were keyed by serviceId alone; selecting a different consumer agent (Nakamoto <-> Kn0w1) exposed one agent's Advisor/Architect input and result under the other agent's selection, and a request resolving after a switch could write into the newly selected agent's view.

notes: Directly analogous to a classic multi-tenant cache-key bug (keying on resource id without tenant id); the constitutional stakes here are higher because the 'tenants' are distinct governed agents and the leaked state is confidentiality-bearing (one agent's advisory request/result surfacing under another).

The discovery/admission-diagnostic view is deliberately NOT covered by this same composite-key pattern — it represents 'the currently selected principal's live eligibility view', a single mutable projection guarded instead by a monotonically increasing generation counter so a stale fetch for a previously selected principal can never overwrite the current one. Both mechanisms serve the same isolation goal via different means suited to different state shapes (per-request history vs. single current view).
